Title: Recently Patched Barracuda Vulnerabilities Exploited in Attacks
Context: Threat actors have started exploiting two recently patched Barracuda vulnerabilities that could be chained to bypass authorization controls and gain root access
Full Text:
Threat actors have started exploiting two recently patched Barracuda vulnerabilities that could be chained to bypass authorization controls and gain root access.

Tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS score of 9.3), the first bug is described as an authentication bypass in Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG).

An attacker with access to the administrative user interface (Admin UI) could trigger it to restore a crafted backup archive and modify the appliance’s configuration.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS score of 8.6), is a command injection weakness affecting Barracuda ESG, Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), Web Application Firewall (WAF), Web Security Gateway (WSG), Message Archiver (BMA), and WAF Control Center (WCC).

An attacker with administrative access to a vulnerable appliance could exploit the security hole to inject OS commands that would be executed with root privileges.

“If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda said on November 2.

A week later, the company updated its advisory to warn that threat actors have been exploiting the two security defects against a small number of organizations.

On Tuesday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to patch them within three days, as mandated by BOD 26-04.

Barracuda and CISA have not shared details on the exploitation, but cybersecurity firm Previdian has observed 17 attempts targeting CVE-2026-116606 between November 9 and November 11. The attacks came from 15 IP addresses in three countries.

All organizations are advised to update their Barracuda products as soon as possible and ensure that their administrative interfaces are not exposed to the internet. Access to them should be restricted only to trusted internal networks.

Title: Barracuda’s email security gateways bitten by make-me-root vulns
Context: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security...
Full Text: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges. “We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory. Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.” The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week. CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface. As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.” CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG). “If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either. We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems. These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities. So if you haven’t already: patch now. ®

Context: The first stems from an Email Security Gateway (ESG) authentication weakness that can be exploited to modify an appliance's global configuration, while the second lets...
Full Text:
Cybersecurity company Barracuda Networks warned that attackers have begun exploiting two recently patched Email Security Gateway (ESG) vulnerabilities that let them run commands with root privileges.

Barracuda released security updates to address the two flaws (tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560) one week ago.

The first stems from an Email Security Gateway (ESG) authentication weakness that can be exploited to modify an appliance's global configuration, while the second lets unauthenticated attackers inject OS commands that execute with root privileges.

Barracuda also said that successful attacks require access to the administrative user interface (Admin UI) of targeted devices and advised customers to restrict access to trusted internal networks and use appropriate network access controls to limit exposure.

"Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device," the company explained.

On Monday evening, Barracuda updated the initial advisory to warn admins that the two flaws are being exploited in attacks targeting a limited number of customers.

"Barracuda immediately initiated a comprehensive remediation process and released security patches for affected products. We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations," it warned.

"If a patch has not been automatically applied, customers should manually apply the appropriate patch as soon as possible. If customers have turned off automatic patching, Barracuda recommends setting devices to automatically receive patches."

Three years ago, Barracuda patched another Email Security Gateway flaw (CVE-2023-7102) that the UNC4841 hacking group exploited in zero-day attacks to execute arbitrary code. The same year, UNC4841 abused another zero-day (CVE-2023-2868) to target Barracuda ESG appliances as part of a series of cyber-espionage attacks.

The company later revealed that the flaw had been exploited as a zero-day for at least seven months, since at least October 2022, to drop previously unknown SeaSpy and Saltwater malware and steal data from compromised devices.

According to cybersecurity firm Mandiant, almost a third of systems breached in the 2023 campaign belonged to government agencies, most of them hacked between October and December 2022.

Barracuda was founded in 2003 and now has more than 200,000 customers worldwide, including small- to medium-sized businesses (SMBs), large enterprises, and managed service providers (MSPs).

Title: Experts Demonstrate Barracuda Email Security Gateway Chain Enabling Root Access Without Login
Context: watchTowr also released a detection tool that checks whether an appliance is vulnerable, but has not published an exploit
Full Text:
Two flaws in Barracuda's Email Security Gateway, an email-filtering appliance, can be chained to run commands on it as root, its highest level of access, with no login required.

The company released patches on Monday, and the security firm watchTowr detailed the attack chain on Thursday.

One flaw, CVE-2026-116606, is an authorization bypass. An unauthenticated attacker can use it to restore a crafted configuration backup and change the appliance's global settings.

The other, CVE-2026-111560, is a command injection. It runs commands as root but normally needs an administrator account, and on the Email Security Gateway the bypass gives an attacker that access. Chained, the two let an attacker reach root with no login.

Affected Products and Fixes

The authorization bypass affects only the Email Security Gateway. The command injection reaches five other products, but on those it still needs an administrator account.

Mandiant, which assigned the two CVE records, rates the bypass 9.3 out of 10 and the command injection 8.6. Barracuda has released a patch for each affected product and lists the fixed firmware in its security advisory. The Email Security Gateway is fixed in version 9.4.0.030 and later.

What to Do

The advisory sets out three steps:

Apply the patch for each affected product, or upgrade to the fixed firmware listed above.

If you cannot patch at once, limit the appliance's administration interface to trusted internal networks.

If you have turned automatic patching off, switch it back on.

How the Chain Works

In its technical analysis, watchTowr traced the chain through the appliance's code. A failed password change returns the attacker a low-privilege role instead of stopping the request, which leaves a backup-restore function open to someone who has not logged in.

That function accepts an uploaded backup, and the restored data includes a timezone value that the appliance later runs as a shell command with root privileges. Barracuda guards backups with a checksum, but the secret used to compute it is built into the code, allowing an attacker to forge a valid checksum. The firm showed the attack by writing a file to the appliance as root.

As of this week, neither flaw appears in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV catalog), and no public report ties either to an attack. watchTowr also released a detection tool that checks whether an appliance is vulnerable, but has not published an exploit.

The Email Security Gateway was hit in the 2023 attacks by a group tracked as UNC4841, which exploited a different flaw, CVE-2023-2868, as a zero-day. That case is unrelated to the two flaws patched this week, and nothing ties the new pair to any attacker.
